Group discussed on Dec 9th, decided we needed more community input in order to refine this.  Is the main goal performance?  Should this be restricted to non-destructive (add-only) requests, so that compensation is more feasible?  User doesn't necessarily want to formulate a package.  Wants to mark a transaction start, do stuff, and end.  How close can we get to that ideal without complicating the implementation too much? In the latter case, if it's done that way, this may be out of scope for the Fedora Respository Project itself.
This is particularly interesting to Virginia as we continue to investigate the use of service bus technology to operate our repository workflows.
The so-called "super method" is a new API-M method that allows a set of API-M methods to be submitted as a single operation, doing all of the work in one transaction.

comments.body:
[Followup from Sourceforge Tracker]
Followup Submitter: pangloss
Logged In: YES
user_id=487398
Originator: YES

2007-07-17

Objective:

To provide a method to support running a batch of API-M
operations as a single atomic operation. Benefits:
atomicity and performance. Atomicity: Fedora clients
would not need to manually compensate if the series of
operations failed part way through. Performance:
a) A single network request vs. many
b) A single database transaction vs. many (transaction
setup/teardown can be expensive)

Basic process:

  • Takes a series of API-M requests in one "package".
  • Starts a transaction
  • Executes each request, in order.
  • Commits and returns a series of corresponding API-M responses.
  • If anything fails along the way, rolls back and throws a fault.

Issues:
Request "package" format?
Response format?
SOAP vs. REST?

[Followup from Sourceforge Tracker]
Followup Submitter: pangloss
Logged In: YES
user_id=487398
Originator: YES

2007-07-19

Decided:

  • SOAP (i.e., API-M)
  • Not recursive
  • Binary attachment support identified as a prerequisite

I don't recall what was decided with respect to what restrictions, if any, we were imposing on the set of permissible methods except for the super method itself.
